"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5312, as a typical value with a document-start rule.

The component's activation is a weak, diffuse readout of the layer's MLP hidden state, with
mean about 0.10 and no simple rule explaining most of its variation. Two patterns do hold
in the data: the first token of each document is always about zero, and the few tokens
right after it are a little above the typical value.
"""

READS = ()

FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0
EARLY_TOKENS = 0.2  # document positions 1 to 4
TYPICAL = 0.1


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:
        k = 0
    else:
        k = carry[1] + 1
    if k == 0:
        value = FIRST_TOKEN
    elif k <= 4:
        value = EARLY_TOKENS
    else:
        value = TYPICAL
    return (doc, k), value

"""Collection-type detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 5314.

The component is about collections. It is large on the names of container types
(List, list, ArrayList, Vec, array, vector, Map, Set, dict, queue, stack), strongest
when the word names a type in code (after new, ::, ->, :, or .util), weaker when it is
English ("the list of", "a set of"). It is also strong on empty list literals ([] or
=[) and on container operations after a dot (.add, .append, .push, .size, .get), and
slightly raised on the token one or two places after a container word. Its output
direction promotes list-like continuations (list, .toList, .addAll, listOf), so it
reads "a collection is being named or built here". Most other tokens sit near zero,
and the large variance inside each class is not explained by anything this program sees.

The weights are the mean activation of each class on sampled training positions. A
word counts only inside its own document, so no carry is needed.
"""

READS = ()

CONTAINERS = {"list", "array", "vector", "vec", "arraylist", "linkedlist", "tuple",
              "map", "set", "hashmap", "hashset", "dict", "dictionary", "collection",
              "queue", "stack", "deque"}
CONTAINER_OPS = {"push", "append", "add", "addall", "size", "get", "put", "insert",
                 "pop", "length", "len", "keys", "contains", "aslist", "includes"}
EMPTY_LITERALS = {"[]", "[];", "[],", "=["}
# Code tokens after which a container word names a type in code.
TYPE_CONTEXT = {"new", "::", "->", ":", ".util"}
W_TYPE, W_OTHER = 9.9, 3.0  # a container word: naming a type in code, or otherwise
W_OP, W_EMPTY, W_NEAR = 3.0, 6.0, 0.7


def _word(token):
    """The bare lowercase word of a token, without spaces, newlines, dots or underscores."""
    return token.strip().lstrip("._").lower()


def _is_container(token):
    return _word(token) in CONTAINERS


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = len(tokens) - 1
    token = tokens[t]
    value = 0.0
    if token.strip() in EMPTY_LITERALS:
        value = W_EMPTY
    elif token.startswith(".") and _word(token) in CONTAINER_OPS:
        value = W_OP
    elif _is_container(token):
        before = tokens[t - 1].strip() if t >= 1 and docs[t - 1] == docs[t] else ""
        value = W_TYPE if before in TYPE_CONTEXT else W_OTHER
    # A token one or two places after a container word, in the same document, is slightly raised.
    for back in (1, 2):
        j = t - back
        if j >= 0 and docs[j] == docs[t] and _is_container(tokens[j]):
            value += W_NEAR
            break
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP down-projection component 5315: a constant near zero.

What the component is: a rank-one piece of layer 15's down_proj. It reads the MLP
hidden vector through one direction, V_c, that is dominated by hidden unit 5315
(about 14% of its squared weight) and spread thinly over ~6000 other units. Its
activation is that read-out times the output direction's norm.

What the data shows: the activation is about zero-mean with std 0.32 and no
simple trigger. Its sign does not follow any token identity, token class (digit,
letter, punctuation, space), previous token, or position in the document: every
such predictor explains about 1% of its variance or less. Its causal importance
is essentially 0 everywhere, and switching it off changes the model's next-token
predictions by almost nothing.

So the honest program is the constant mean activation. It explains no variance,
and it moves the model's output essentially as much as switching the component
off does.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = 0.0033


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """The activation at this position: the constant mean."""
    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Disjunction words: a weak, mostly-unexplained component of layer 15's MLP output.

What it does: it goes negative on disjunction words, "or" and its translations
(nor, ou, oder, или, 或, または, lub, eller, oppure), and stays near 0 elsewhere.
The strongest and most common case is " or" (mean about -0.6). Nothing else here is
modelled.

Why this is all it does: over 16k training rows the component's activation is
spiky and only weakly tied to the current token. Its spikes sit in many
contexts (code indentation, " =" in dictionary counters, "new", "update", ...),
and no token-level rule captures them. A small MLP over the previous 8 tokens
explains only about 3% of its variance, so this program explains well under 1%.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Disjunction words, lowercased and without the leading space.
DISJUNCTIONS = {"or", "nor", "ou", "oder", "или", "或", "或者", "または", "lub", "eller", "oppure"}

# Typical activation on these words: " or" averages about -0.6.
VALUE = -0.5
# Everywhere else, the component's average level (its mean is about +0.035).
BASELINE = 0.035


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    # The newest token, decoded alone, is the token this activation is read at.
    word = prefix.token_strings[prefix.position].strip().lower()
    return carry, (VALUE if word in DISJUNCTIONS else BASELINE)

"""Layer 15 MLP hidden unit 5317, read through its down_proj component 5317.

The component's activation is (MLP hidden value x V) times the norm of its output vector. Its
V is dominated by the MLP hidden unit 5317 itself, so this is that unit's value, scaled. The
unit is signed and heavy-tailed: std about 0.55, mostly within +-2, with rare values near +-20
to +-40. It is not explained by the current token alone, by position in the document, by
repetition or induction, or by simple token-class features. The weak tendencies found: strongly
negative values are a little more common on code- and file-name-like tokens (".md", ".go",
"_test", backslashes), and strongly positive values a little more common on ordinary prose
words. Those tails are two-sided, so the average value barely moves by class.

This program predicts the typical value of each of three token classes, so its predictions
are near zero everywhere. It explains almost none of the variance (about 0.002 on eval): the
component is close to unpredictable from the prefix's surface text.
"""
import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

CODE_LIKE = re.compile(r"[\\_/{};=()\[\]<>#$&|@*]|\.(md|go|py|js|ts|yml|yaml|json|txt|c|h|java|rs|sh)\b|[a-z][A-Z]")
PROSE_WORD = re.compile(r"\s[A-Za-z]+")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if CODE_LIKE.search(token):
        return carry, 0.002
    if PROSE_WORD.fullmatch(token):
        return carry, -0.055
    return carry, -0.006

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5318: a near-inert, token-idiosyncratic direction.

What it is: one rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. Its activation
(the hidden unit combination it reads, times its output norm) is roughly zero-mean,
Gaussian-like noise with std about 0.27 at every position, and it hardly depends on
the text: the current token, the previous token, the position in the document, or
the document as a whole explain only a few percent of its variance. Its causal
importance is essentially 0 everywhere, and switching it off changes the model's
next-token predictions by about 1e-6 nats.

What this program does: it predicts 0 at every position. That is the mean of the
activation, so it explains (almost) none of the variance, and it leaves the model
essentially unchanged, like switching the component off.

Simple alternatives (not used): a per-token mean table with shrinkage explains about
3% of the variance on held-out text, but it is a table of arbitrary token ids with no
concept behind it, and its tokens (e.g. 'ran', 'cd', 'workspace') do not form a
readable class.
"""

READS = ()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # The activation has no readable rule; its best readable guess is its mean, 0.
    return carry, 0.0

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5320: a dense, context-bound feature with no
readable token rule. This program predicts only its typical value.

What it is: the activation is (MLP hidden vector . V_c) * ||U_c||. V_c's largest entry is
hidden unit 5320 of this layer's MLP (0.29; about 17% of its squared norm), and the
activation correlates with that unit at r = 0.47. The activation is small and roughly
symmetric (std 0.31, mean -0.02). It almost never passes the causal-importance threshold,
and switching it off barely moves the model's predictions.

What this program does: it predicts the typical value. Every document's first token is
exactly 0 in the data, so the program predicts 0 there, and -0.02 (the mean) at every other
token. It reads no token identity: token identity, previous token, simple token classes
and document position explain almost none of the variance (held-out R^2 about 0.02 at best,
from a 150k-entry table, which is not a readable explanation).

What it misses: the real variance is token-level and context-dependent (lag-1
autocorrelation 0.34) and comes from the model's residual stream, not from a short rule.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_VALUE = -0.02  # typical activation away from a document's first token
FIRST_TOKEN_VALUE = 0.0  # the activation is zero at every document's first token


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first_in_doc = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, (FIRST_TOKEN_VALUE if first_in_doc else MEAN_VALUE)

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5321: a weak, diffuse read-out of the MLP hidden
units (mostly unit 5321). Its activation is near 0 almost everywhere, with typical
values of +-0.3, and no simple concept accounts for most of its variance.

What this program does: it predicts the component's average value (about +0.02) on
ordinary text, and a clearly negative value on the digits and colons of a
"file:line" or "node:internal/...:line" location inside a stack trace, the one
pattern where the component is reliably strongly negative. Everything else is
left at the average.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MEAN = 0.02
# a stack-trace location: "node:internal/...:" or "name.ext:" directly before a line number
LOCATION = re.compile(r"(node:|\.\w+:)[\w/.\-:]*$")
DIGITS_AND_COLONS = re.compile(r"[\d:]+")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    line = carry or ""
    if len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        line = ""
    text = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    line = (line + text).split("\n")[-1][-120:]
    if DIGITS_AND_COLONS.fullmatch(text) and LOCATION.search(line):
        return line, -1.0
    return line, MEAN

"""Explain-by-rules for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 5322.

This component is a dense, noisy feature: its activation has mean 0.15 and spread 0.9,
and no simple rule explains most of it. What it does track, on average, is the kind of
word being read:

* nouns score high, most of all plural nouns (people, societies, cells), nouns after a
  determiner or quantifier (the, these, all, your), and concrete nouns for people, groups,
  animals, food, objects and artifacts;
* a noun right after a pronoun (he, she, they, it, who) scores low;
* verbs, auxiliaries and other function words score low (is, can, will, that, of).

The program predicts a weighted sum of these word-class flags. The weights are least
squares fits to 8,192 training rows. Word classes come from WordNet and small word lists.
"""

import re

import wordnet

READS = ()

DETERMINERS = set(
    "the a an this that these those each every all some many most few several both any no "
    "my your our their his her its one two three".split()
)
PRONOUNS = set("he she they it we i you who which".split())
FUNCTION_WORDS = DETERMINERS | PRONOUNS | set(
    "of in on at to for with by from as into about over under between through and or but "
    "not if so than then there here when while because also is are was were be been being "
    "am has have had do does did can could will would should may might must shall".split()
)
PEOPLE_AND_THINGS = {
    "noun.person", "noun.group", "noun.animal", "noun.food",
    "noun.object", "noun.artifact", "noun.plant", "noun.body",
}

# intercept, plural noun, noun after determiner, noun after pronoun,
# noun after and/to/or, concrete noun, verb, function word, non-letter token
WEIGHTS = (0.129, 0.432, 0.349, -0.287, -0.085, 0.142, -0.188, -0.154, 0.018)


def word_flags(token, previous):
    """Word-class flags for the current token, given the previous token (same document)."""
    word = token.strip().lower()
    is_word = re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]+", word) is not None
    pos = wordnet.parts_of_speech(word) if is_word else frozenset()
    noun = "noun" in pos
    plural = noun and len(word) >= 4 and word.endswith("s")
    concrete = noun and bool(wordnet.categories(word, "noun") & PEOPLE_AND_THINGS)
    verb = "verb" in pos and not noun
    after_det = previous in DETERMINERS
    after_pron = previous in PRONOUNS
    after_and_to = previous in ("and", "to", "or")
    return (
        1.0,
        float(noun and plural),
        float(noun and after_det),
        float(noun and after_pron),
        float(noun and after_and_to),
        float(noun and concrete),
        float(verb),
        float(word in FUNCTION_WORDS),
        float(not is_word),
    )


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    previous = ""
    if len(prefix.token_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]:
        previous = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower()
    flags = word_flags(token, previous)
    value = sum(w * f for w, f in zip(WEIGHTS, flags))
    return carry, float(value)

"""Change-of-state detector (layer 15 MLP, component 5323).

The component fires on the word that expresses a change of state: strongest on
"become / became / becomes / becoming" (and their translations), weaker on
"now" (as in "X is now ..."), on verbs of beginning and growing ("began",
"grow", "turned", "emerged", "gained"), on progress adverbs ("suddenly",
"eventually", "increasingly"), and on "into" or "to" right after a verb of
change or motion ("came to", "grow to", "turned into", "switched to").
Everywhere else it is near zero.

This is a lexicon: each group gets the mean activation it has on training text.
It explains only about a tenth of the variance; most of the rest is the
context in which these words sit, which a word list cannot see.
"""

READS = ()

BECOME = {"become", "becomes", "became", "becoming", "成为", "成了", "变得", "变成",
          "стала", "становится", "menjadi", "變得"}
BEGIN_GROW = {"began", "begun", "begin", "begins", "start", "started", "starts",
              "grow", "grew", "growing", "grown", "turn", "turned", "turns",
              "emerge", "emerged", "emerging", "emerges", "gain", "gained", "gaining",
              "develop", "developed", "developing", "develops", "evolve", "evolved",
              "join", "joined", "joining", "joins", "increase", "increased", "increasing",
              "decided", "decide", "decides", "learned", "learn", "reached", "reach",
              "reaches", "acquire", "acquired", "add", "added", "adds", "adding", "开始"}
PROGRESS_ADV = {"increasingly", "suddenly", "eventually", "subsequently", "thereafter",
                "soon", "later", "finally", "still", "again", "longer", "then", "until",
                "newly", "gradually", "quickly", "逐渐", "突然", "越来越", "теперь",
                "jetzt", "ahora", "newfound", "renewed"}
CHANGE_VERBS = {"come", "came", "comes", "coming", "grow", "grew", "grown", "growing",
                "rise", "rose", "risen", "rising", "turn", "turned", "turns", "turning",
                "switch", "switched", "switches", "switching", "shift", "shifted",
                "transition", "convert", "converted", "transform", "transformed",
                "change", "changed", "increase", "increased", "decrease", "decreased",
                "reduce", "reduced", "drop", "dropped", "fall", "fell", "fallen", "move",
                "moved", "evolve", "evolved", "develop", "developed", "upgrade",
                "upgraded", "promote", "promoted", "restore", "restored", "return",
                "returning", "start", "starting", "went", "go", "going", "back",
                "transferred", "expanded", "added", "add", "get", "got", "getting",
                "changes", "changed", "reduces", "moves", "moving", "returned"}

# Mean activation per group, fitted on training text.
BECOME_VALUE = 12.4
NOW_VALUE = 5.0
BEGIN_GROW_VALUE = 2.8
PROGRESS_ADV_VALUE = 1.9
NEW_VALUE = 2.4
INTO_VALUE = 4.1
TO_AFTER_CHANGE_VALUE = 4.8


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    before = prefix.token_strings[-2].strip().lower() if same_doc else ""
    if word in BECOME:
        value = BECOME_VALUE
    elif word == "now":
        value = NOW_VALUE
    elif word in ("to", "到") and before in CHANGE_VERBS:
        value = TO_AFTER_CHANGE_VALUE
    elif word in ("into", "onto"):
        value = INTO_VALUE
    elif word in BEGIN_GROW:
        value = BEGIN_GROW_VALUE
    elif word in PROGRESS_ADV:
        value = PROGRESS_ADV_VALUE
    elif word == "new":
        value = NEW_VALUE
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, float(value)

"""Heuristic for layers.15.mlp.down_proj component 5324.

What it does: the component is weak and diffuse. Its clearest positive activity is on
Japanese and Korean predicate material: the stems, verb and adjective endings and
auxiliaries that build a verb phrase (ている, ない, ること, よう, いい, できる, する, た,
Korean 할, 수, 해 ...), where the sentence is still mid-predicate. Hiragana particles
are moderate; の and は are low. Hangul is mildly positive. Latin text, Han characters,
Cyrillic and punctuation are near zero, and Latin words are mostly noise around zero.

The program reads only the current token and predicts its activation from its script
and a short list of Japanese auxiliaries. Values are rough category means.
"""
import re

READS = ()

HIRAGANA = re.compile(r"[぀-ゟ]")
HANGUL = re.compile(r"[가-힯]")

# Japanese verb/adjective endings and auxiliaries (predicate material).
AUXILIARIES = {
    "ている", "している", "っている", "ない", "ます", "ました", "ません", "たい",
    "よう", "ようだ", "こと", "もの", "ること", "できる", "できない", "いい", "良い",
    "ある", "がある", "である", "する", "して", "した", "し", "て", "た", "る",
    "れる", "られる", "せる", "させる", "って", "った", "いた", "いて", "ろう", "う",
}
# Topic and genitive particles, which the component largely ignores.
WEAK_PARTICLES = {"の", "は"}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip()
    if token in AUXILIARIES:
        value = 3.0
    elif token in WEAK_PARTICLES:
        value = 0.3
    elif HIRAGANA.search(token):
        value = 1.75
    elif HANGUL.search(token):
        value = 0.8
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, value

"""Spatial-relation words, signed by inside vs. outside.

Component: layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5325, a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection.
Its activation is near zero on most tokens, but it swings strongly on words that name a
spatial relation between two things: prepositions such as "in", "inside", "within",
"through" (the located thing is inside or part of the place), and "over", "across",
"beside", "near", "around", "along" (the located thing is outside, above or next to
the place). The determiner right after such a preposition ("in THE", "over A") carries
the preposition's sign. "of" after an edge noun ("bank of", "shore of", "side of",
"north of") is strongly negative; "of" after a part noun ("part of", "inside of",
"interior of") is positive.

The program is a small lexicon of those words with hand-set signs and strengths, and
the output is scaled to match the component's typical size. It ignores context beyond
the previous word, and so it captures only the broad sign and the shape of the spikes.
What it misses: the size of a spike depends on the wider sentence (the same "over" is
about -38 in "a bridge over the water" and +5 in "amortized over 30 years"), and most
of the component's variance lies in small activations on ordinary tokens that no
simple rule here predicts. Explained variance on held-out rows is about 3%.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Preposition -> signed strength. Positive: containment or being a part of the place.
# Negative: adjacency, crossing, or being external to the place.
PREP = {
    "inside": 2.5, "within": 2.0, "throughout": 1.5, "in": 1.0, "into": 1.0,
    "through": 1.0, "under": 0.8, "beneath": 1.0, "dans": 1.0, "в": 1.0,
    "outside": -0.5, "against": -0.3, "along": -0.7, "above": -0.8, "across": -0.8,
    "sur": -0.8, "over": -1.0, "around": -1.2, "near": -2.0, "surrounding": -2.0,
    "beside": -4.0, "overlooking": -10.0,
}
# Determiners that follow a preposition and inherit its sign.
DETS = {"the", "a", "an", "its", "their", "his", "her", "my", "our", "your", "this"}
# Nouns after which "of" marks an edge or boundary (negative) or a part (positive).
EDGE_NOUNS = {"side", "sides", "bank", "banks", "shore", "shores", "edge", "coast",
              "mouth", "north", "south", "east", "west", "border", "end", "bottom"}
PART_NOUNS = {"part", "parts", "inside", "interior", "portion", "portions", "region",
              "heart", "middle", "center", "scope", "contents"}
SCALE = 0.7  # the typical size of the component's activation per unit of the lexicon
DET_GAIN = 2.0  # a determiner after a preposition carries about twice its sign


def _word(text: str) -> str:
    return text.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = _word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    same_doc = len(prefix.document_ids) > 1 and prefix.document_ids[-2] == prefix.document_ids[-1]
    prev = _word(prefix.token_strings[-2]) if same_doc else ""
    if word in PREP:
        value = PREP[word]
    elif word in DETS:
        value = DET_GAIN * PREP.get(prev, 0.0)
    elif word == "of" and prev in EDGE_NOUNS:
        value = -4.0
    elif word == "of" and prev in PART_NOUNS:
        value = 1.5
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, SCALE * value

"""Layer 15 MLP, down_proj component 5326: a weak, mostly unpredictable signal.

What it is: a rank-one piece of the MLP down projection that reads almost only one hidden
unit (neuron 5326). Its output direction promotes " or" / "或" and suppresses " and" / "和"
in the logit lens, so a negative activation means "the model leans toward a conjunction
(and, a list comma) next", and a positive one leans toward "or".

What this program does: it predicts a small value from the token's place in its document
and its surface type. It is only a rough sketch: the activation is mostly context-driven,
and simple rules explain well under 1% of its variance.
  - The first few tokens of a document (positions 1-3) lean positive.
  - Later, lowercase words, quotes, brackets and blank tokens lean slightly positive.
  - Later, capitalised words (names), word pieces that continue a word, digits,
    "and"/"or", commas, periods and newlines lean slightly negative, matching the
    "and"/list-continuation reading.
Everything else is 0.
"""

READS = ()

EARLY = {1: 0.25, 2: 0.15, 3: 0.1}
POSITIVE_LATER = ('"', "'", "`", "(", "[", "{")
NEGATIVE_LATER = ("and", "or", ",", ".")


def is_name_or_piece(tok, s):
    """A capitalised word (a name), or a word piece that continues a word (no leading space)."""
    if s[:1].isupper() and s.isalpha():
        return True
    return s.isalpha() and not tok.startswith(" ")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[1] != doc:
        n = 0
    else:
        n = carry[0] + 1
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    s = tok.strip()
    if n in EARLY:
        value = EARLY[n]
    elif n < 4:
        value = 0.0
    elif (tok.startswith(" ") and s.isalpha() and s.islower()) or tok in POSITIVE_LATER or s == "":
        value = 0.05
    elif is_name_or_piece(tok, s) or s.isdigit() or s in NEGATIVE_LATER or "\n" in tok:
        value = -0.04
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return (n, doc), value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj component 5327: a diffuse, near-constant activation.

MODAL_OR_PERFECT = {" can", " will", " may", " must", " should", " shall", " could", " would",

def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2] if same_doc else ""

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5341: a weak "pointing the reader somewhere" detector.

What the component does: its activation is a linear readout of the layer-15 MLP hidden
state (mostly hidden unit 5341). It is near zero almost everywhere, with a small diffuse
spread. Its clearest large responses are negative, in web or UI instructions that send the
reader to a destination: "Simply click it and you will be [taken] [to] a page", "This will
take you [to]", "it leads [to]", "links [to]", "refers [patients] to". There the activation
reaches -5 to -24, usually on the verb (leads, refers, opens, brings) or on the word that
follows a click/link/take cue (to, you, a, page).

This program predicts that pattern in a simple way: a fixed negative value on a
"pointing" verb, and on a follow-up word (to, you, a, ...) shortly after a navigation cue
in the same document. Everywhere else it predicts 0. It captures only the strongest
pattern, and most of the component's variance comes from diffuse small values it does not
model.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Words that direct a reader to a place: the cue a following "to" depends on.
CUE_WORDS = frozenset(
    {
        "link", "links", "click", "clicks", "clicking", "clicked",
        "take", "takes", "taken", "lead", "leads", "led", "refer", "refers",
        "referring", "redirect", "redirected", "direct", "directs", "navigate",
        "opens", "brings", "send", "sends", "sent",
    }
)
# Verbs that point somewhere themselves (their own activation is clearly negative).
POINTING_WORDS = frozenset(
    {"lead", "leads", "led", "refer", "refers", "referring", "brings", "opens"}
)
# Words that usually come right after a cue, where the destination is named.
FOLLOW_WORDS = frozenset({"to", "you", "a", "it", "them", "be", "the", "page", "and", ","})

VALUE = -0.3  # typical activation at those spots
WINDOW = 3  # how many tokens after a cue the follow-up word may come


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    tokens = prefix.token_strings
    docs = prefix.document_ids
    t = prefix.position
    word = tokens[t].strip().lower()
    if word in POINTING_WORDS:
        return carry, VALUE
    if word in FOLLOW_WORDS:
        for j in range(max(0, t - WINDOW), t):
            if docs[j] == docs[t] and tokens[j].strip().lower() in CUE_WORDS:
                return carry, VALUE
    return carry, 0.0

"""Counterfactual-clause detector for layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5342.

Most of this component's activation is small, diffuse noise. Its clearest signal is a
negative tail on the words that open a contrary-to-fact ("unreal") conditional, after a
modal such as "would", "could", "might" or "should":
    "...would have been X if it had not..."   ("if", "had" strongly negative)
    "...would not be said were it not for..."  ("were")
    "...если бы", "wenn", "si", "hätte" in the same role.
Words of absence or exclusion ("without", "non-", "normal", "before", "prior", "unless")
and other conditional markers get a weak negative value. Everywhere else the value sits
near the average.

The program looks back a few words in the same document for a modal cue.
"""

READS = ()

MODAL_CUES = {"would", "could", "might", "should", "wouldn", "couldn", "'d"}
MARKERS = {"if", "were", "had", "wenn", "si", "бы", "hätte", "hätten", "wäre"}
ABSENCE = {"without", "non", "normal", "absence", "prior", "before", "single", "unless", "otherwise"}
WINDOW = 6
STRONG, WEAK, BASE = -1.1, -0.15, 0.04


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    t = prefix.position
    word = prefix.token_strings[t].strip().lower()
    recent = [
        prefix.token_strings[i].strip().lower()
        for i in range(max(0, t - WINDOW), t)
        if prefix.document_ids[i] == prefix.document_ids[t]
    ]
    if word in MARKERS and any(w in MODAL_CUES for w in recent):
        value = STRONG
    elif word in MARKERS or word in ABSENCE:
        value = WEAK
    else:
        value = BASE
    return carry, value

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5343: a diffuse, near-silent feature.

What it is: a single rank-one piece of the MLP down projection. It reads the MLP
hidden vector and is dominated by hidden unit 5343 of layer 15 (about 31% of its
weight norm sits on that one unit). Its activation is roughly 0.44 * that hidden unit,
with a typical size of about 0.3 and a mean of about -0.04.

What the data show, measured on ~2M training tokens:
- Its activation has no readable token or context signature. Predicting it from the
  token identity explains about 1% of its variance, from a coarse token class (digit,
  punctuation, CJK, word) about 0.1%, from position in the document about 0.04%,
  and from whether a token repeats earlier text about 0%. Surprisal and entropy of
  the model's own next-token prediction are uncorrelated with it.
- At the first token of each document it is essentially zero.
- The decomposition never counts it as important: its causal importance is about
  6e-7 on average and never passes 0.1, and switching it off changes the model's
  next-token predictions by about 1.6e-6 nats per position.

So the program predicts the component's baseline value everywhere, zero at the first
token of a document. It does not explain the component's variance; it only reproduces
its mean, which is why it has no real explanatory content.
"""

READS = ()

BASELINE = -0.04  # the component's mean activation over the training sample
FIRST_TOKEN = 0.0  # at a document's first token the activation is about zero


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    first = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]  # a document's first token (or a row's first)
    return None, (FIRST_TOKEN if first else BASELINE)

"""Eagerness-to-please phrasing, as a rule over the last few tokens.

p-82af68dd@100000 layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5344 is one rank-one piece of the MLP's down
projection. Most of its activation is diffuse, small and sign-mixed, and nothing
readable predicts that part. Its large positive spikes come from one register: a
word of pleasure, eagerness or gratitude, and the "to" after it, as in "I'd be happy
to help", "I'm thrilled to have the opportunity to", "I look forward to hearing
from you", "We eagerly anticipate the opportunity to", "greatly appreciated".

This program reads the current token and the two before it (same document only):
  - a strong feeling word (happy, glad, delighted, honored, thrilled, excited,
    grateful, proud, lucky ...) itself:                              +4
  - "to" right after such a word or "forward" (the big spike):       +10
  - a softer courtesy word (great, nice, love, pleasure, honor,
    opportunity, hope, eagerly, appreciated ...):                     +1.5
  - "to" right after a softer courtesy word:                          +3
  - the one or two tokens after a strong feeling word:                +1.5
  - anything else:                                                    0

It does not model the negative spikes (C-like code identifiers and punctuation),
which are real but sparse and not predictable from a few words.
"""

READS = ()

STRONG = {
    "happy", "glad", "delighted", "pleased", "honored", "honoured", "thrilled",
    "excited", "grateful", "thankful", "proud", "lucky", "fortunate", "blessed",
    "appreciate",
}
SOFT = {
    "pleasure", "privilege", "privileged", "honor", "opportunity", "great", "nice",
    "wonderful", "love", "hope", "welcome", "thank", "thanks", "eager", "eagerly",
    "anticipate", "appreciated", "greatly", "enjoy", "sorry", "forward",
}
TO_AFTER_STRONG = STRONG | {"forward"}

W_STRONG = 4.0
W_TO_STRONG = 10.0
W_SOFT = 1.5
W_TO_SOFT = 3.0
W_AFTER = 1.5


def _word(token):
    return token.strip().lower()


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    doc = ids[-1]

    def back(k):
        # the word k tokens back, or "" if it lies in an earlier document
        if len(ids) > k and ids[-1 - k] == doc:
            return _word(prefix.token_strings[-1 - k])
        return ""

    cur = _word(prefix.token_strings[-1])
    prev1, prev2 = back(1), back(2)
    if cur in STRONG:
        value = W_STRONG
    elif cur == "to" and prev1 in TO_AFTER_STRONG:
        value = W_TO_STRONG
    elif cur == "to" and prev1 in SOFT:
        value = W_TO_SOFT
    elif cur in SOFT:
        value = W_SOFT
    elif prev1 in STRONG or prev2 in STRONG:
        value = W_AFTER
    else:
        value = 0.0
    return carry, float(value)

"""Layer 15 MLP unit 5345 (down_proj component 5345), read as a word-level "pairs and sides" feature.

What it does: the component's activation is mostly near zero, with rare large positive
values where the text is about two sides or parties relating to each other ("the parties",
"mutual", "neither side", "counsel"), and negative values on words that mark a pair or a
contrast ("two", "between", "same", "different", "respectively").

Its output direction promotes words such as "mutually", "both", "neither", "respectively"
and "each other", so it tends to fire on the words that come just before such a reciprocal
phrase. This program does not model that context: it only looks at the current word, and
the word-level rule explains almost none of the variance (see the explanation).
"""

READS = ()

# Words about sides or parties that relate to each other: the component goes up.
PARTY_WORDS = {"parties", "party", "sides", "mutual", "mutually", "neither", "counsel", "respective"}

# Words that mark a pair or a contrast between things: the component goes down.
PAIR_WORDS = {"two", "between", "same", "different", "differ", "respectively", "opposite", "another"}

RESTING = -0.05  # the component's typical value on ordinary words


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()
    if word in PARTY_WORDS:
        value = 2.0
    elif word in PAIR_WORDS:
        value = -0.4
    else:
        value = RESTING

"""Layer 15 MLP down_proj, component 5346: a diffuse neuron with two weak tendencies.

Its activation is near zero most of the time (mean 0.02, std 0.33) with rare large
values. Almost all of its variance is not explained by any word, position or document
rule we tried; a per-token lookup, a bag of the previous 16 tokens and these two rules
together explain well under 2% of it. What the two rules do capture:

- Negative in narration that orders or repeats events ("then", "next", "again",
  "another", "later", "before", ...). A decaying count of those words in the current
  document sets how far below zero it goes.
- Positive in code and maths: the share of code-like tokens among the last 16 tokens.

The coefficients are least-squares fits on 8k training rows; they are not tuned on eval.
"""

import re
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS = ()

SEQUENCE_WORDS = frozenset(
    "then next again another second third previous before until later first "
    "subsequent after finally once following each while last prior".split()
)
CODE_MARK = re.compile(r"[{}()\[\];=+*/<>_]|def |return")
DECAY = 0.8  # how fast the sequence count fades, per token
WINDOW = 16  # tokens over which the code share is measured


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    if carry is None or prefix.position == 0:
        state, recent = 0.0, ()
    else:
        state, recent = carry
    if prefix.position > 0 and prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        state, recent = 0.0, ()
    token = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    state = DECAY * state + (token.strip().lower() in SEQUENCE_WORDS)
    recent = (recent + (bool(CODE_MARK.search(token)),))[-WINDOW:]
    code_share = sum(recent) / len(recent)
    value = 0.018 - 0.05 * state + 0.043 * code_share
    return (state, recent), value

"""Component 5348 of layers.15.mlp.down_proj, predicted as a word-shape rule.

Almost all of this component's activation is one MLP hidden unit of layer 15 (unit 5348),
read through the component's input direction. That unit is near zero in most places and is
mostly negative in non-English text. It goes most negative on the last piece of an inflected
word: Russian adjective and noun endings (-ный, -ной, -ных, -ого, ...) and Greek final sigma.
It is also negative on a few function words ("de", "para", "pour", "для", "des", "с").
Its positive side is weak and scattered, so this rule predicts only the negative side and
leaves everything else near its small typical value.

Rule, from the token just read and the one before it:
  - first token of a document: 0
  - function word from the list below: its typical value
  - Cyrillic word ending (whole token is an inflection): strongly negative
  - other Cyrillic pieces: moderately negative, less so when starting a word
  - Greek final sigma: strongly negative
  - other letter pieces: slightly negative, less so when they start a word
  - everything else (punctuation, digits, spaces): near zero
"""
import re

READS = ()

RU_ENDING = re.compile(
    r"ный|ная|ное|ные|ного|ной|ном|ным|ных|ную|ными|ый|ая|ое|ые|ого|ому|ой|ую|ых|ым|ыми|ом|ов|ев|ей|ие|ия|ии|ием|ью|ам|ах|ами"
)
WORD = re.compile(r"[^\W\d_]+")
CYRILLIC = re.compile(r"[Ѐ-ӿ]+")
PREPOSITIONS = {
    " de": -1.4,
    " para": -1.7,
    " pour": -1.7,
    " для": -1.9,
    " с": -1.0,
    " des": -0.8,
    " les": -0.9,
    " en": -0.6,
    " и": -0.6,
    " du": -0.5,
}


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    tok = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    if prefix.position == 0:
        return carry, 0.0
    prev = prefix.token_strings[-2]
    if tok in PREPOSITIONS:
        return carry, PREPOSITIONS[tok]
    if WORD.fullmatch(tok) is None:
        return carry, -0.1
    if CYRILLIC.fullmatch(tok):
        if RU_ENDING.fullmatch(tok):
            return carry, -2.0
        if WORD.fullmatch(prev):
            return carry, -0.6
        return carry, -0.4
    if tok == "ς":
        return carry, -4.0
    if WORD.fullmatch(prev):
        return carry, -0.2
    return carry, -0.1

What it does: the unit is mostly near zero, but it goes clearly negative on prepositions
that open an adjunct phrase hanging off a clause or noun:
  - "by" almost anywhere, most strongly in agent phrases after a noun ("the reduction by
    the Company", "the denial by the courts");
  - other prepositions right after a comma or a past participle / -ed word
    (", in a very ...", ", as he had ...", "born in", "obtained by", "described in").

This program predicts a fixed negative value at those positions and 0 everywhere else. It
captures only the average shape. Most of the activation's variance is context-specific and
is not explained by the words around it, so this explains a very small share of it.

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Prepositions that can open an adjunct phrase.
PREPOSITIONS = frozenset(
    "in at as for through under during on with from into of to between over after within via".split()
)
BY_VALUE = -0.8  # mean activation on "by", the most negative preposition
ADJUNCT_VALUE = -0.4  # mean activation on other prepositions after a comma or -ed word


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    word = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower()

    if word == "by":

What it does, plainly: no short rule captures its variation. Its activation is a small,
dense, roughly symmetric signal (mean about 0.03, std about 0.32) built from the MLP's
hidden units; the single hidden unit 5350 of that layer carries about a quarter of its
variance, and the rest is spread over thousands of units. It is near zero on the first
token of each document (about 0.004).

Token identity, position, repetition within the document, character class, leading space,
and running document statistics (digit, punctuation, non-ASCII fractions) predict it poorly:
held-out variance explained is about 1 percent or less. Its causal importance is about 1e-7,
so the component is effectively inert on the model's outputs.

So this program is a baseline: it predicts the component's typical value, a constant near
its mean, and zero on document-initial tokens. It explains the component's average level,
not its variation.

READS = ()

MEAN = 0.03  # the component's average activation on ordinary (non-document-initial) tokens


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    ids = prefix.document_ids
    doc_start = len(ids) == 1 or ids[-1] != ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if doc_start else MEAN

"""Word-piece program for p-82af68dd@100000/layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5351.

The component is a weak, high-variance feature. Its large negative values sit on
pieces of words that a tokenizer has split apart: the second or later piece of a
long, rare or foreign word (e.g. "Büror|ä|umen", "Vijayal|ak|shmi"). Numbers and
punctuation are mildly negative, ordinary whole words are slightly negative when
common and slightly positive when rare or unknown. The first token of a document
is exactly 0. Nothing here predicts the sign of the large spikes well, so this
explains only a small part of the variance.
"""

import regex
from wordfreq import zipf_frequency

READS = ()
LANGS = ("en", "de", "fr", "es", "it", "pt", "nl", "ru", "sv", "fi", "pl", "cs", "hu", "tr", "id")


def common(word):
    """Whether any of a few languages' wordfreq lists knows the word (Zipf >= 3.5)."""
    return max(zipf_frequency(word.lower(), lang) for lang in LANGS) >= 3.5


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    if prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]:
        return carry, 0.0
    s = prefix.token_strings[-1]
    st = s.strip()
    if st == "":
        return carry, -0.007
    if regex.fullmatch(r"\p{N}+", st):
        return carry, -0.05
    if not regex.fullmatch(r"\p{L}+", st):
        return carry, -0.017
    if s[:1] != " ":
        return carry, -0.053
    return carry, (-0.02 if common(st) else 0.01)

training rows, about -0.014. It does not explain the activation's variance; it is the
honest baseline, and switching the component off has almost no effect on the model.
"""
from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# Mean activation over training positions (about -0.014; std 0.36).
MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.014


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):

    return carry, MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Component L15 MLP down_proj:5354 -- an "engineering / patent-register" feature.

What the component is: its read direction is dominated by MLP hidden unit 5354 of layer 15
(SiLU(gate) * up for that unit; weight 0.88 of its norm 1.36), so it tracks that neuron. It is large and
positive inside technical prose, the style of patent specifications and engineering
manuals ("the valve is mounted to the housing", "the coolant flows through the pump"), and
near zero or slightly negative in ordinary prose and in code. Within that prose it is
strongest on the machine, electrical and fluid words themselves.

What this program does, in plain terms:
  1. Keeps a running share of how many words so far in the document are engineering or
     patent-claim words (the LEXICON below). Shrunk toward 0 for short documents.
     This tracks the "technical register" of the text.
  2. Adds a bonus when the current token is itself such a word.
Its prediction is therefore: (technical share so far) * 25 + (1.1 if this word is technical).
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MACHINE_PARTS = set(
    """valve motor shaft piston brake clutch rotor gear pump engine cylinder housing tube
    pipe spring rod blade screw roller nozzle chamber tank duct inlet outlet bearing torque
    ignition steering connector coupling clamp latch drum conveyor compressor mill welding
    molding mold plate sheet pin filter lens hinge wheel axle crank belt pulley actuator""".split()
)
ELECTRICAL = set(
    """circuit voltage resistor capacitor coil sensor battery signal electrode switch
    amplifier wire cable chip processor memory magnet electrical electric current pulse
    transistor semiconductor diode led emitter detector detecting sensing controller
    switching waveform volt circuits signals sensors electrodes batteries motors""".split()
)
FLUID_THERMAL = set(
    """fluid gas fuel coolant water air vapor liquid oil combustion exhaust heat cooling
    pressure temperature flow coating vacuum laser beam light optical wave frequency
    vibration friction hydraulic adhesive polymer solution mixture material materials
    steel glass""".split()
)
PATENT_WORDS = set(
    """embodiment embodiments invention preferably wherein comprises comprising configured
    mounted disposed coupled connected positioned formed adapted plurality substantially
    thereby preferred arranged attached rotates movable adjustable predetermined embodied
    portion surface layer element apparatus assembly device devices system unit member
    arrangement""".split()
)
LEXICON = MACHINE_PARTS | ELECTRICAL | FLUID_THERMAL | PATENT_WORDS

SHRINK = 10  # pseudo-count: the share is hits / (words so far + SHRINK)


def is_technical(token: str) -> bool:
    word = token.strip().lower()
    if word.endswith("s") and word[:-1] in LEXICON:
        return True
    return word in LEXICON


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[0] != doc:  # a new document: start the running share afresh
        hits, count = 0.0, 0
    else:
        _, hits, count = carry
    hit = 1.0 if is_technical(prefix.token_strings[-1]) else 0.0
    share = hits / (count + SHRINK)
    value = 25.0 * share + 1.1 * hit
    return (doc, hits + hit, count + 1), value


def main() -> None:
    """Demo: the technical-register score of a short passage, token by token."""
    text = "The valve is mounted to the housing, and the coolant flows through the pump."
    words = text.replace(",", " ,").replace(".", " .").split(" ")
    hits, count = 0.0, 0
    for word in words:
        hit = 1.0 if is_technical(word) else 0.0
        print(f"{word!r:14} share={hits / (count + SHRINK):.3f} hit={hit:.0f}")
        hits, count = hits + hit, count + 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

with heavy tails: it spikes to about +-10 to +-20 on roughly 1 position in 400, with either
sign. Spikes come when the gate opens strongly; the sign comes from the up projection.

What the program does: it predicts only the typical value for the kind of the current token
(code-like, CJK, Latin-script word, or other). It does not predict the spikes. Nothing simple
does: the identity of the current or previous token explains no held-out variance, and a
bag of the preceding 16 tokens explains about 1%.
"""

import regex

READS = ()

CODE = regex.compile(r"[{}();=<>_/\\#\[\]]|\.\w")
CJK = regex.compile(r"\s?[\p{Han}\p{Hiragana}\p{Katakana}]+")
WORD = regex.compile(r"\s?\p{Latin}+")

# Mean activation per kind of token, measured on training text.
MEAN = {"word": -0.065, "code": -0.021, "cjk": -0.089, "other": -0.033}


def kind(token):
    if CODE.search(token):
        return "code"
    if CJK.fullmatch(token):
        return "cjk"
    if WORD.fullmatch(token):
        return "word"
    return "other"


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    return None, MEAN[kind(prefix.token_strings[-1])]

"""Component p-82af68dd@100000 layers.15.mlp.down_proj:5373, predicted as a near-constant.

What the component is: a single rank-one piece of layer 15's MLP down projection. It reads the
MLP's hidden state h (6144 units) along one direction and writes along one direction, so its
activation is (h . read direction) * (write norm). That read direction is spread across many
hidden units; the largest single share is hidden unit 5373 itself, which correlates about 0.44
with the activation, and the rest is smeared over hundreds of units.

What it does in the model: almost nothing. Its causal importance is ~0 on every token of the
corpus, and switching it off changes the next-token distribution by ~1.6e-6 nats per position.

What the activation looks like: diffuse, mean about -0.066, std about 0.29, roughly symmetric.
At a document's first token it is ~0. Elsewhere no token identity, token class, position, or
short context of token classes predicts it (out-of-sample variance explained is ~0), so the
program predicts the mean for every other position.
"""

READS = ()

MEAN_ACTIVATION = -0.066
"""The component's average activation on non-initial tokens."""


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    # A document's first token starts a new document: the component reads ~0 there.
    starts_doc = prefix.position == 0 or prefix.document_ids[-1] != prefix.document_ids[-2]
    return carry, 0.0 if starts_doc else MEAN_ACTIVATION

"""Activation of one MLP hidden unit's write (layer 15, down_proj component 5374).

What it does: predicts a small baseline (0.015), raised by 0.014 for each mathematical or
step-by-step rewriting word ("number", "sum", "fraction", "becomes", "remaining",
"transform", ...) among the last 64 tokens of the same document.

Why: this component's activation is diffuse and mostly unpredictable from words. Over
sampled text it averages about 0.02 with standard deviation about 0.37. Its mean and
spread do rise in quantitative text: the mean goes from about 0.015 in passages with no
such words to about 0.09 in the densest ones (more than 6 in 64 tokens), and the RMS goes
from about 0.36 to about 0.7. Many of its largest spikes (up to about 20) fall in such
passages, e.g. fraction, Collatz and rectangle-area lessons. This rule captures only the
shift in the mean. It does not predict the spikes or the sign of the typical value, which
depend on context that a word list cannot describe.
"""

from collections.abc import Mapping

READS: tuple[str, ...] = ()

MATH_WORDS = frozenset(
    """number numbers integer integers digit digits sum sums fraction fractions equation
    equations polynomial quotient divide divides divided divisible prime matrix theorem proof
    solve variable variables function value becomes become remaining transform transformed
    transformation reduce reduced simplify convert converted factor factors product remainder
    modulo sequence integral derivative algebra expression""".split()
)
WINDOW = 64  # tokens back, within the same document
BASE = 0.015  # mean activation with no math words nearby
PER_WORD = 0.014  # added for each math word in the window


def step(carry, prefix, upstream: Mapping):
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    recent = carry[1] if carry is not None and carry[0] == doc else ()
    is_math = prefix.token_strings[-1].strip().lower() in MATH_WORDS
    recent = (recent + (is_math,))[-WINDOW:]
    return (doc, recent), BASE + PER_WORD * sum(recent)

"""L15 MLP down_proj component 5375: a sentence-end detector.

The component is quiet on most tokens but fires on the punctuation that closes
a sentence: ".", "?", "!", "。", "？", "！" and the full-width colon "：". It is
strongest on the first sentence end of a line or paragraph, and it fades with
each further sentence end in that line. Its size grows with how long the
sentence was, is raised by first- and second-person or argumentative wording
("I", "you", "we", "not", "maybe", ...), and is lowered by code-like text and
by digits. Commas get a small negative value (",") or positive value ("，").
A sentence end that closes a medium-length line (10 to 40 tokens in) gets a
bonus; one at the very start of a line gets a penalty.

Predicts the component's activation, the size of its write, as a number per token.
"""
import math
import re

READS = ()

SENTENCE_END = set(".?!。？！：")
PERSONAL = re.compile(r"\b(I|you|your|we|me|my|maybe|really|think|know|what|want)\b", re.I)
CODE = re.compile(r"[/_{}()\[\];=<>#\\`]|https?")
DIGIT = re.compile(r"\d")


def step(carry, prefix, upstream):
    """Activation at the newest token. carry = (text since last sentence end,
    sentence ends so far in this line, tokens in this line, document id)."""
    doc = prefix.document_ids[-1]
    if carry is None or carry[3] != doc:  # a new document starts fresh
        carry = ("", 0, 0, doc)
    text, ends, line, _ = carry
    t = prefix.token_strings[-1]

    if t in SENTENCE_END:
        value = -0.5 if t == "." else -0.15  # "." is weaker than the other marks
        value += 0.38 * math.log(1 + len(text))  # longer sentences fire more
        value += 1.27 / (1 + ends)  # first sentence end of a line fires most
        value += 0.84 * bool(PERSONAL.search(text))  # conversational, argumentative
        value -= 0.62 * bool(CODE.search(text))  # code-like text fires less
        value -= 0.73 * bool(DIGIT.search(text))  # numbers fire less
        if 10 <= line < 40:  # ends a medium-length line of prose
            value += 0.5
        elif line < 6:  # ends a very short line
            value -= 0.3
        return ("", ends + 1, line + 1, doc), value

    if "\n" in t:  # a new line resets the line's sentence count
        return ("", 0, 0, doc), 0.0
    value = -0.15 if t == "," else 0.7 if t == "，" else 0.0
    return (text + t, ends, line + 1, doc), value
